Motion from the fundamentals · for the curious engineer

eiωte^{i\omega t}eiωt

the atom of motion

One equation — a point going around a circle — turns out to be the atom of motion. A thrown football, a falling rock, a spinning ball, a planet in orbit, a vibrating beam, a circuit, a control loop: all of them are this one object, dialed to different settings. Here is the whole idea, built from scratch.

Act I
The question
A football does three motions at once. One idea, or three?

A thrown football does three things at once

Throw a tight spiral and follow a single scuff on the leather. Three motions are tangled into its path:

  • it sails downfield at a steady clip,
  • it rises and falls in an arc under gravity,
  • it spins around the ball's long axis.

Are these three separate pieces of physics, stapled together? Or one idea wearing three costumes? The whole point of what follows: they are one object — and once you see it, you will recognize the same object in half of your engineering courses.

Act II
The atom
Meet eiωte^{i\omega t}eiωt, and see why it is the natural unit of any smooth motion.

The turning arrow

Start with the equation itself. Picture an arrow pinned at one end to the centre of a circle — like a clock's hand, or a compass needle — free to swing, its tip riding around the rim. That swinging arrow, of length 1 and turning at a steady rate ω\omegaω, is eiωte^{i\omega t}eiωt. We will call it simply the arrow for the rest of the page. Its two coordinates are carried on the one object:

eiωt  =  cos⁡ωt  +  i sin⁡ωt\displaystyle e^{i\omega t} \;=\; \cos\omega t \;+\; i\,\sin\omega teiωt=cosωt+isinωt

Why a circle and not a straight line? Because of the iii. Multiplying by iii is a 90° turn, so the velocity is always perpendicular to the arrow — it can never move the tip outward or inward, only around. Drag the speed below and watch.

Engineers have a name for this rotating arrow: a phasor. You will meet it again in AC circuits, signals, and vibrations — the same arrow, every time.

It is the one motion that differentiates into itself

Take the time-derivative of the turning arrow:

ddt eiωt  =  iω eiωt\displaystyle \frac{d}{dt}\,e^{i\omega t} \;=\; i\omega\,e^{i\omega t}dtd​eiωt=iωeiωt

Differentiating does not change its shape — it only scales and rotates it (by ω\omegaω, and by 90°). The arrow is the eigenfunction of the derivative: the fixed point of "rate of change." That is the deep reason it shows up everywhere a thing changes smoothly in time. Pocket this — it is the seed of the whole engineering payoff at the end.

A quantity whose rate of change is proportional to itself is an exponential — that is the definition. Make the proportionality imaginary (iωi\omegaiω) and "growth" becomes "rotation." Real exponents grow or decay; imaginary exponents go in circles. We will need both.
Act III
Take the arrow apart
Its series terms are the motions; how far it turns picks which you see.

Expand the arrow once, and the motions fall out

Write out where the tip has gone after a time ttt, term by term (this is just the exponential's power series):

eiωt  =  1  +  iωt⏟glide  −(ωt)22⏟fall  −  i(ωt)36  +  ⋯\displaystyle e^{i\omega t}\;=\;1\;+\;\underbrace{\textcolor{#69f0ae}{i\omega t}}_{\text{glide}}\;\underbrace{\textcolor{#ff6b6b}{-\tfrac{(\omega t)^2}{2}}}_{\text{fall}}\;-\;\tfrac{i(\omega t)^3}{6}\;+\;\cdotseiωt=1+glideiωt​​fall−2(ωt)2​​​−6i(ωt)3​+⋯
  • The first move of a turning tip is a straight nudge sideways — a glide. (Order ttt: constant velocity.)
  • The next is a pull inward that grows like t2t^2t2 — a fall. (Order t2t^2t2: constant acceleration.)
  • Keep every term and the nudge-plus-fall curls back into a closed loop — the spin. (All orders.)

So glide, fall, and spin are not three things. They are term 1, term 2, and the whole sum of one arrow. Add the terms one at a time below: one gives a line, two give a parabola, more curl it toward the true circle.

One number: how far it turns = rate × time

A thrown football, it turns out, hides two of these arrows: a small, fast one — the spin — and an enormous, sluggish one — the trajectory, the path the ball itself takes. What sorts them, and what decides whether each shows only a sliver of motion (a glide and a fall) or the whole loop (a spin), is a single number: how far the arrow turns while you watch — its rate times the elapsed time.

We never "throw away" the higher terms by hand. For a barely-turning arrow they simply have not grown yet; for the fast spin they are full size and stay. Same series, two windows.

Act IV
Put it in the world
A force makes the arrow; gravity is one such force; speed turns the fall into an orbit.

A force writes the equation; the arrow solves it

What sets ω\omegaω in the first place? A force. Write zzz for the position of the arrow's tip — the arrow itself, a single point in the plane. A pull toward the centre means its acceleration always points back at where it is, sized by ω2\omega^2ω2:

z¨  =  − ω2 z\displaystyle \ddot z \;=\; -\,\omega^2\, zz¨=−ω2z

And the arrow already obeys this. Differentiating it multiplies by iωi\omegaiω (that was Act II); do it twice and you multiply by (iω)2=−ω2(i\omega)^2 = -\omega^2(iω)2=−ω2 — exactly this equation. So a centre-seeking force goes in, and the turning arrow z=eiωtz=e^{i\omega t}z=eiωt comes out:

z¨  =  d2dt2 eiωt  =  (iω)2 eiωt  =  − ω2 eiωt  =  − ω2z\displaystyle \ddot z \;=\; \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\,e^{i\omega t} \;=\; (i\omega)^2\,e^{i\omega t} \;=\; -\,\omega^2\,e^{i\omega t} \;=\; -\,\omega^2 zz¨=dt2d2​eiωt=(iω)2eiωt=−ω2eiωt=−ω2z

And when the turning slows toward nothing — ω→0\omega\to 0ω→0, with the arrow growing huge so its tip keeps its speed — it stops looping and degenerates into its first terms: a straight glide, or, under a steady inward pull, a fall. The polynomials of freshman physics are just the zero-frequency limit of the same equation.

Constraint vs. force. The spin looks "automatically perfect" because the ball is rigid: each point is a bead on a rigid hoop, pinned to its circle, with the inward force supplied for free — exact for any ω\omegaω. The arc's shape, by contrast, is whatever gravity produces — a circle only when finely tuned (an orbit). Enforced circle vs. earned circle.

Gravity is centripetal: g=RΩ2g = R\Omega^2g=RΩ2

This is that slow trajectory arrow in close-up — the same arrow as ever, now grown to a great length RRR and creeping around at a slow rate Ω\OmegaΩ, a clock's hand at the top of a huge circle, swinging down. Watch only its drop below the top.

After the hand turns through an angle Ωt\Omega tΩt, the part of it still pointing up is Rcos⁡ΩtR\cos\Omega tRcosΩt — so the tip has fallen by the rest:

drop(t)  =  R−Rcos⁡Ωt  =  R (1−cos⁡Ωt)\displaystyle \text{drop}(t)\;=\;R-R\cos\Omega t\;=\;R\,(1-\cos\Omega t)drop(t)=R−RcosΩt=R(1−cosΩt)

And cos⁡Ωt\cos\Omega tcosΩt is nothing new — it is the real, even-powered half of the arrow's own series from Act III,

cos⁡Ωt  =  Re⁡(eiΩt)  =  1−(Ωt)22+(Ωt)424−⋯\displaystyle \cos\Omega t\;=\;\operatorname{Re}\big(e^{i\Omega t}\big)\;=\;1-\tfrac{(\Omega t)^2}{2}+\tfrac{(\Omega t)^4}{24}-\cdotscosΩt=Re(eiΩt)=1−2(Ωt)2​+24(Ωt)4​−⋯

so subtracting it from 1 cancels the constant, and a factor of RRR leaves the drop as a series. The leading term is a parabola; everything after it is the circle's tail — the extra wiggles that keep a circle from being a parabola, tiny here only because Ωt\Omega tΩt is small:

drop(t)  =  12RΩ2t2⏟the parabola — the fall  −  RΩ424t4+⋯⏟the circle’s tail\displaystyle \text{drop}(t)\;=\;\underbrace{\tfrac12 R\Omega^2 t^2}_{\text{the parabola — the fall}}\;-\;\underbrace{\tfrac{R\Omega^4}{24}t^4+\cdots}_{\text{the circle's tail}}drop(t)=the parabola — the fall21​RΩ2t2​​−the circle’s tail24RΩ4​t4+⋯​​

And here is where RΩ2R\Omega^2RΩ2 actually comes from — circular-motion kinematics, not algebra. A tip circling at radius RRR and rate Ω\OmegaΩ has a fixed speed, RΩR\OmegaRΩ, and a fixed inward acceleration, RΩ2R\Omega^2RΩ2 (that inward RΩ2R\Omega^2RΩ2 is just the −Ω2z-\Omega^2 z−Ω2z from "a force writes the equation," at radius RRR). Those two are nothing but the arrow's first two terms — and the first two terms of any motion are its velocity and its acceleration. So to make this arrow be the throw, we just match them to it: the tip should move sideways at the launch speed, and accelerate downward at ggg. At the top of the circle "inward" points straight down, so the centripetal pull simply is the downward pull, and the match reads:

RΩ2=g⟹gravity is the pull holding the ball on its trajectory-circle.\displaystyle R\Omega^2 = g \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{gravity is the pull holding the ball on its trajectory-circle.}RΩ2=g⟹gravity is the pull holding the ball on its trajectory-circle.

Now make it exact. Hold RΩ2=gR\Omega^2=gRΩ2=g and put R=g/Ω2R=g/\Omega^2R=g/Ω2 back into the series — every term becomes ggg times a power of Ω\OmegaΩ:

drop(t)=g[t22−Ω2t424+Ω4t6720−⋯]=12g t2⏟no Ω left−gΩ224t4+⋯⏟spare Ω’s\displaystyle \text{drop}(t)=g\Big[\tfrac{t^2}{2}-\tfrac{\Omega^2 t^4}{24}+\tfrac{\Omega^4 t^6}{720}-\cdots\Big]=\underbrace{\tfrac12 g\,t^2}_{\text{no }\Omega\text{ left}}-\underbrace{\tfrac{g\Omega^2}{24}t^4+\cdots}_{\text{spare }\Omega\text{'s}}drop(t)=g[2t2​−24Ω2t4​+720Ω4t6​−⋯]=no Ω left21​gt2​​−spare Ω’s24gΩ2​t4+⋯​​

The g/Ω2g/\Omega^2g/Ω2 used up the Ω2\Omega^2Ω2 in the first term exactly, leaving it Ω\OmegaΩ-free — pure 12gt2\tfrac12 g t^221​gt2. Every other term is left holding spare factors of Ω\OmegaΩ. So as the arrow grows huge and slow (Ω→0\Omega\to0Ω→0), those spare-Ω\OmegaΩ terms go genuinely to zero, while 12gt2\tfrac12 g t^221​gt2 cannot budge — its ggg is pinned. The tail isn't sleeping now; it is starved out, and the circle's drop becomes the parabola exactly, drop(t)=12gt2\text{drop}(t)=\tfrac12 g t^2drop(t)=21​gt2.

So the textbook fall is not an approximation we reach by ignoring a tail — it is the destination. A finite circle is approximately a parabola (tail tiny but present); the infinite, infinitely-slow circle is the parabola (tail gone for good). The standard equation is exact; the circle simply sheds its extra wiggles to land on it.

Throw it faster and the circle becomes the Earth

The trajectory-circle's radius grows with launch speed, R=v2/gR=v^2/gR=v2/g. Throw harder, bigger circle, flatter arc, farther before it lands. Orbit is the moment that circle grows to the size of the planet — the ball then curves down exactly as fast as the ground curves away, and never lands. That happens at

v=g R⊕≈7.9 km/s(about 400×a quarterback).\displaystyle v=\sqrt{g\,R_\oplus}\approx 7.9\ \text{km/s}\quad(\text{about } 400\times \text{a quarterback}).v=gR⊕​​≈7.9 km/s(about 400×a quarterback).

Fire the cannon below at increasing speed and watch the parabola open into a circular orbit — that orbit genuinely is the arrow — and, faster still, into a wide ellipse and then escape. Past the circle it is the same gravity, only the speed dialed up; those wider paths belong to the 1/r21/r^21/r2 world we fence off at the end, not to a single turning arrow. (Newton's cannonball, 1687.)

Act V
The whole landscape
Every oscillation at once — and why this runs through your whole engineering curriculum.

The football, recomposed: two arrows

Now the throw collapses. The glide and the fall were never separate — they are the two coordinates of one slow arrow. The spin is a second, fast arrow riding on top.

x=vxt ,  y=−12gt2⏟two coordinates of the slow arrow  +  r eiωt⏟the fast spin arrow\displaystyle \underbrace{\textcolor{#69f0ae}{x=v_x t}\,,\ \ \textcolor{#ff6b6b}{y=-\tfrac12 g t^2}}_{\text{two coordinates of the slow arrow}}\ \ +\ \ \underbrace{\textcolor{#4dd0e1}{r\,e^{i\omega t}}}_{\text{the fast spin arrow}}two coordinates of the slow arrowx=vx​t,  y=−21​gt2​​  +  the fast spin arrowreiωt​​

Three motions you can watch; two turning arrows behind them; one idea. The only difference between the arrows is how far each turns — a sliver versus seventeen loops.

Why those two coordinates? They are the arrow's two halves. The height is its real (even-powered, cosine) part — the fall we just did. The sideways position is its imaginary (odd-powered, sine) part, and it starves its tail by the identical trick, taken to its own slow limit (rate Ω′\Omega'Ω′):

sideways(t)=Rsin⁡Ω′t  →  R=vx/Ω′    vx[t−Ω′26t3+⋯]  →  Ω′→0    vx t\displaystyle \text{sideways}(t)=R\sin\Omega' t\;\xrightarrow{\;R=v_x/\Omega'\;}\;v_x\Big[t-\tfrac{\Omega'^2}{6}t^3+\cdots\Big]\;\xrightarrow{\;\Omega'\to0\;}\;v_x\,tsideways(t)=RsinΩ′tR=vx​/Ω′​vx​[t−6Ω′2​t3+⋯]Ω′→0​vx​t

The vx/Ω′v_x/\Omega'vx​/Ω′ strips the lone Ω′\Omega'Ω′ off the leading term; every higher term keeps spare Ω′\Omega'Ω′'s and dies. And notice the symmetry that fixes those two conditions: the power of Ω\OmegaΩ in each is just the order of the term it protects — the glide is order t1t^1t1, so RΩ′=vxR\Omega'=v_xRΩ′=vx​; the fall is order t2t^2t2, so RΩ2=gR\Omega^2=gRΩ2=g. One arrow, read two ways, each leaning on the same limit.

One honest note on that slow arrow. We start it at the very peak of the arc, which is why the height reads as a clean −12gt2-\tfrac12 g t^2−21​gt2 with no rising half. A real throw just starts the arrow a little before the top — a head start that is simply a phase, ei(Ωt+φ)e^{i(\Omega t+\varphi)}ei(Ωt+φ) — and reading its height then gives the full rise-and-fall, vy t−12gt2v_y\,t-\tfrac12 g t^2vy​t−21​gt2. So even the launch angle is nothing new: it is just where the arrow begins on its circle.

The whole catalog: the complex plane of λ\lambdaλ

Real motions are never the pristine ideal — a spin slowly bleeds off energy to drag; a struck bell rings and dies. So widen the exponent from a pure rotation iωi\omegaiω to a general complex rate λ\lambdaλ — its imaginary part the frequency, its real part the growth or decay. The single template eλte^{\lambda t}eλt now covers everything, and the whole landscape is just where λ\lambdaλ sits in the plane:

  • On the imaginary axis (Re⁡λ=0\operatorname{Re}\lambda=0Reλ=0): pure, eternal rotation — an ideal spin, a circular orbit.
  • In the left half (Re⁡λ<0\operatorname{Re}\lambda<0Reλ<0): a ring that decays — a real spin winding down, a shock absorber, an RLC circuit.
  • At the origin: the degenerate drift and fall — the polynomials.
  • In the right half (Re⁡λ>0\operatorname{Re}\lambda>0Reλ>0): runaway growth — instability, feedback squeal.

Drag λ\lambdaλ around and watch the motion it produces — this is exactly the sss-plane you will use in controls and circuits (left half stable, right half unstable). The frequency is set by one ratio in any real system: ω=stiffness/inertia\omega=\sqrt{\text{stiffness}/\text{inertia}}ω=stiffness/inertia​.

This plane is hiding in your whole curriculum

The reason to care: that one template eλte^{\lambda t}eλt is the solution of every linear, constant-coefficient differential equation — which is the first model engineers reach for in almost every field. The same picture, renamed:

Vibrations / dynamics: a mass–spring–damper is mx¨+cx˙+kx=0m\ddot x + c\dot x + kx = 0mx¨+cx˙+kx=0. Its motion is eλte^{\lambda t}eλt; the real part of λ\lambdaλ is the damping, the imaginary part the damped natural frequency.
Circuits: an RLC loop obeys the identical equation with L,R,CL,R,CL,R,C. Ringing, damping, resonance — same λ\lambdaλ.
Controls: the "poles" of a system are literally points λ\lambdaλ in this plane. Left half = stable (decays), right half = unstable (blows up). The root-locus is this exact picture.
Signals: the Fourier and Laplace transforms write any signal as a sum of these arrows, ∫eλt d(⋯ )\int e^{\lambda t}\,d(\cdots)∫eλtd(⋯). The whole subject is bookkeeping for turning arrows.

Whether those courses are ahead of you or behind you, the surprise is the same: these are not four new things. They are this one arrow, four more times — and probably nobody told you it was one arrow.

And where the single arrow stops being enough

Everything so far assumed the force is proportional to displacement — the linear world, where one arrow does the job. Real forces curve away from that: gravity is 1/r21/r^21/r2, a real spring stiffens when stretched far, a pendulum swung hard is not a clean sine. Then a single eλte^{\lambda t}eλt no longer suffices — you get blends of frequencies (harmonics), then, pushed harder, chaos. The turning arrow is the first and dominant story of motion; the rest of physics is the corrections to it.

Act VI
One idea
It was one arrow all along.

eiωte^{i\omega t}eiωt: how far it turns is the whole story

A point going around a circle. Expand it and its terms are the kinds of motion. Dial how far it turns and you slide from a spin, to a fall, to a glide; dial the speed and the fall opens into an orbit; let it decay and you have every real oscillation; sum many of them and you have any signal at all. A force only ever chooses which arrow you are looking at.

every motion is the same object:   e λt\;e^{\,\lambda t}eλt

The math is the catalog of every motion there could be; a physical law only ever points at one of them — and a thrown football points at three at once.

The exponential is the atom of motion in any universe with smooth time. All we ever do — for a football, a planet, a circuit, a beam — is plug in the physics we happen to have.
